title: The Wise Poet of Damascus
summary: In Damascus lived an eminent scholar and poet named Al-Muntajib, celebrated for his profound learning in philosophy and his unyielding defense of the rights of the common people...
full_text:
In Damascus lived an eminent scholar and poet named Al-Muntajib, celebrated for his profound learning in philosophy and his unyielding defense of the rights of the common people. When a tyrannical governor was appointed over the province, who extorted heavy taxes and imprisoned all who criticized his decrees, Al-Muntajib’s friends warned him that his life was in immediate peril.

To save his life without compromising his principles, Al-Muntajib chose a daring path: he donned a ragged tunic decorated with peacock feathers, walked through the streets carrying a hobby-horse made of a palm reed, and began reciting strange, whimsical verses in the marketplace. The citizens whispered: 'Alas! The great philosopher has lost his wits through excessive study!'

The suspicious governor summoned the 'mad poet' to the citadel to interrogate him.

'Why do you ride a stick of palm wood, O philosopher?' asked the governor with mocking laughter.

Al-Muntajib bowed with comical reverence: 'My lord, my palm-reed steed has many virtues over your Arabian stallions: he requires no oats, never kicks his groom, carries me directly toward the truth, and never participates in the robbery of the poor!'

The governor frowned, unsettled: 'And what say you of my royal government?'

The poet chanted with brilliant madness:
'The shepherd who devours his flock shall find his shears grow dull,
The palace built on tears and blood is nothing but a skull;
The crown upon a tyrant's head is fashioned out of glass,
And through the gates of history his shadow soon shall pass!'

The courtiers gasped, but the governor, believing the man was genuinely insane, merely laughed in contempt and ordered him released: 'He is a harmless lunatic; let him ride his palm-stick in the streets!'

Al-Muntajib preserved his life and freedom, continuing to guide the oppressed citizens with allegorical verses until the tyrant was deposed, proving that the guise of folly can be the sharpest sword of wisdom.
moral: Apparent madness is often the shield of wisdom, protecting truth from the wrath of oppressive tyrants.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "The Mad Lover"?
options: Presence of mind and quiet wisdom triumph over brute strength.
Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
